title: The Ravenswood Kitchen Where Wallace Abbott Made His Own Granules
dek: In 1888 a young Chicago doctor who distrusted the pills he could buy began making dosimetric granules at home.

story.event: Deciding to manufacture his own alkaloidal granules at home in Ravenswood
story.summary: In 1888 Wallace Abbott, a 30-year-old physician who ran the People's Drug Store in Ravenswood, north of Chicago, began making his own dosimetric alkaloid granules because those he could buy dissolved poorly and were costly. By the company's own history, first-year sales were $2,000; he advertised to doctors from 1891 and incorporated the Abbott Alkaloidal Company in 1900. Demand for alkaloidal products fell from 1912, and the firm turned to synthetic drugs, becoming Abbott Laboratories in 1915.
paragraphs: In 1885 Wallace Abbott, newly qualified from the University of Michigan's medical school, borrowed $1,000 to buy a doctor's practice in Ravenswood, then a small village north of Chicago. He and his wife, Clara, lived in a frame house where he also opened the People's Drug Store, selling remedies such as his own toothache drops.

A frequent visitor, the physician and salesman William Thackeray, won him over to dosimetric medicine, the teaching of the Belgian doctor Adolphe Burggraeve. Instead of fluid extracts mashed with mortar and pestle, whose strength nobody could know, Burggraeve wanted measured doses of purified plant alkaloids. Liquid extracts also spoiled. Not everyone was convinced: when Thackeray urged Parke-Davis to make granules, its general manager replied that the idea would fail and, if it did not, "it would mean the ruin of the fluid extract business." Abbott began buying granules from Thackeray's own Chicago firm, but found many did not dissolve as claimed, and other makers' pills were scarce and dear.

In 1888, aged 30, he decided to make his own. According to the company's history he worked in the kitchen of the couple's small apartment, though its timelines also place the work at the back of the drugstore. He followed Burggraeve's handbook and masked the bitterness by rolling pills in round-bottomed pans or dipping them, stuck on pins, in sugary liquid. He wrote that he considered "a handy case of active remedies in a convenient form far superior to the time-honored methods of bottles full of nauseous mixtures."

By the company's own count, sales were $2,000 that first year and $8,000 by 1890. His parents moved nearby; their kitchen became a spare laboratory, and his father filled bottles and pasted labels. In 1891 Abbott placed his first advertisement aimed at doctors. He incorporated as the Abbott Alkaloidal Company in 1900, selling shares to other doctors. The granules did not last: by 1912 demand for alkaloidal products was falling, in 1914 the firm turned to synthetic medicines, and in 1915 it became Abbott Laboratories.

quote.text: It is true, that what is settled by custom, though it be not good, yet at least it is fit; and those things which have long gone together, are, as it were, confederate within themselves; whereas new things piece not so well; but though they help by their utility, yet they trouble by their inconformity.
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Bacon notes that new things help by their usefulness yet trouble by not fitting what custom has settled. Abbott's granules troubled the fluid-extract trade, but within about twenty-five years his own firm was setting them aside for synthetic drugs.

reflection: Abbott's complaint was specific: granules that did not dissolve as promised. He did not set out to found a large company; he set out to stop giving patients medicine he could not trust. The company kept that standard and let go of the method, turning to synthetic drugs while he was still alive.

Bacon's warning cuts both ways. New things trouble people before they help, and Abbott's granules unsettled an older trade. Then they became the settled thing that had to give way. It may help to hold your methods more loosely than your reasons for them, and to let a good method be retired without feeling that you have failed.
invitation: Name one tool you use every day that you do not quite trust. Write down exactly what is wrong with it in one sentence, and leave the fixing for another day.

research_notes: Where the granules were first made: the company's own history book says 'in the kitchen of his small apartment' (and its 1889 timeline entry says the kitchen sink of the apartment he and Clara shared), while its 1888 timeline entries and abbott.com say 'in the rear of' or 'at' the People's Drug Store; the drugstore was in the frame house where the couple lived, so the accounts may describe the same building. The Gale company history also says the kitchen. The story gives the kitchen and notes the drugstore version. The slate's 'apartment' is the book's word. Outcome numbers: all early sales figures ($2,000 in 1888, $4,500 in 1889, $8,000 in 1890, $100,000 in 1898) come from Abbott's own history and are attributed as the company's count; the Gale history gives $200,000 by 1905 and was not used. The company history is a celebratory corporate book; the Parke-Davis manager's reply is reported there second-hand (to Thackeray) and is attributed. The book is inconsistent about when the firm was named the Abbott Alkaloidal Company (1891 in one timeline, 1894 in another and in the narrative), so the story gives only the 1900 incorporation, which the Gale history confirms. The Gale history says Abbott heard of solid alkaloids from a Belgian surgeon in 1888; the company book says Thackeray converted him after founding his Metric Granule Company in 1887; both name Burggraeve's dosimetric approach, and the story uses the book's sequence. The 1912 decline, 1914 switch and 1915 renaming come from the company's timeline. The book is read through the text that its online flipbook loads (the flipbook page itself shows only the title without JavaScript). Bacon's essay concerns innovation in states and customs generally; it is applied here by analogy.
